translations.text: Truly, every man needs to consider for himself the journey of his soul, and how grave it will be when death comes and separates the kinsmen who were together before, body and soul!
For a long time afterwards the spirit receives from God himself either punishment or glory, according to what that earthly vessel did for it before in the world.

The spirit, crying out in its sorrows, must come again and again, every seven nights, to find the body that it long wore before. It must do this for three hundred years, unless the King of nations, almighty God, the Lord of hosts, wishes to bring about the end of the world sooner.

Then, full of care, the spirit calls out in a cold voice and speaks grimly to the dust: "Lo, you dust, you dreary one, why did you torment me, you filth of the earth, all withered away, you likeness of clay!
You gave little thought to what would become of your soul's state once it had been led out of the body!

What, do you blame me, accursed one? Truly, you food for worms, you gave little thought, when you went about filled with all your lustful horrors, to how you must lie in the earth as a feast for worms!
Lo, before, in the world, you gave little thought to how long it is from then until now!

Lo, the angel from the heavens above sent a soul into you, by the hand of the almighty Creator himself, from his majesty, and he bought you with the holy blood. And you bound me with hard hunger and held me captive in the torments of hell!
I lived inside you. I could not get out of you, enclosed in flesh as I was, and your sinful lusts pressed hard on me.
Very often it seemed to me that it would be thirty thousand years until your death-day. Always I waited in hardship for the two of us to part. And now the end is not very good!
You were proud with feasting and full of wine, you swaggered in your glory, and I was thirsting for the body of God, for the drink of the spirit.

For you did not consider here in life, while I had to live in you in the world, that you had been begotten strong through flesh and through sinful lusts and were sustained through me, and that I was the spirit in you, sent from God.
Never did you save me from such hard torments of hell, because of your desire for your own needs.
You will have to suffer shame for my [?] on that great day when the Only-begotten gathers together all mankind.

Now that I alone have gone out of you, by the hand of the very one who sent me before, you are no dearer to any living person as a companion than the black raven is: not to mother or father or any kinsman.
Now neither the red ornaments, nor gold, nor silver, nor any of your goods can take you away from here, nor your bride's ring, nor your wealth of halls, nor any of the goods you once owned,
but here the bones must wait, stripped bare and torn from the sinews, and I, your soul, must often seek you out against my will to revile you with words, as you did to me.
Now you are dumb and deaf, and your joys are worth nothing.

Yet I must, of necessity, seek you out by night, wounded by sins, and then soon turn away from you again at cockcrow, when holy men sing songs of praise to the living God, and go to seek the dwellings which you have assigned to me here,

[?] and the impious dwelling-place. And here many earthworms will chew you, black creatures, greedy and ravenous, tearing at you painfully. The possessions that you showed off to people here on earth are worth nothing at all.
Therefore it would have been very much better for you than having all the riches of the earth (unless you had given them away to the Lord himself)
if at the beginning you had become a bird, or a fish in the sea, or a beast on earth looking for food, a field-roaming animal without wisdom, or the worst of the wild beasts in the wilderness, [?]

[?] [would that you had been] there as God wished, yes, even though you were the grimmest of the race of worms, there as God wished, rather than that you ever became a man on earth or should ever receive baptism.
when you must answer for us both on that great day, when the wounds will be revealed to men which sinful men committed long ago in the world,

[?] when the Lord himself, the Creator of the heavens, will hear the deeds of every man, and will hear from the voice of every man's mouth [the] requital for wounds. But what will you say to the Lord there on the Day of Judgement?
Then no limb grown on the body will be so small that you will not have to give account for each one separately, when the Lord is stern at the judgement. But what shall the two of us do?
then afterwards we two must together endure such miseries as you assigned to us here before!"
In this way it reproaches the flesh-hoard. Then it must go away, troubled by its deeds, to seek the abyss of hell, not the joys of heaven at all.
The dust lies where it was. It cannot promise the sad spirit any answer, help or comfort.
The head is split apart, the hands are pulled out of joint, the jaws gape, the palate is torn apart, the sinews are sucked away, the neck is gnawed through, the fingers have fallen apart.
Fierce worms strip the ribs. Its tongue is torn into ten pieces as comfort for the hungry ones, so that it cannot trade insulting words with the weary spirit.
The worm whose jaws are sharper than a needle is called Gifer ("Greedy"). He forces his way into the grave first of all,

so that he tears the tongue apart, bores through the teeth and eats through the eyes from above into the head. He opens a way to the feast for the others, as food for worms, when the weary body has grown cold, the body that it long clothed with garments.
Then it is the worms' food, carrion in the earth. That may serve as a reminder to every person, to everyone who is wise of mind!
It is more hopeful when the holy soul travels to the flesh, wrapped in comfort.
That errand is found more blessed in spirit. With joy it gladly seeks the clay vessel that carried it for a long time before.
Then the spirits speak good words, wise and victorious, and in this way they truly greet the body with joy:
"Dearest friend, although worms still greedily attack you, now your spirit has come, beautifully adorned, from my Father's kingdom, wrapped in honours.
"Oh, my lord, if only I could lead you with me, so that the two of us might see all the angels and the glory of the heavens, just as you appointed for me here before!
You fasted on earth and filled me with God's body and with the drink of the spirit.
You were in poverty, but you gave me plenty of what I desired.

So you need not be ashamed of what you gave me when the sinful and the righteous are separated on the great day. Nor need you regret here in life any of all that you gave me, at the meeting place of men and angels.
You humbled [?] yourself before men and raised me up into eternal joy.
Therefore I shall always long, dearest of men, hard in my mind, because I know that you are in these humiliations, a feast for worms; but God willed that you should ever choose such a loathsome bed.
I would tell you, then, not to grieve, because the two of us will be gathered together at God's judgement.
Afterwards we two may then enjoy it together and be exalted in the heavens.
We two need not be anxious at the Lord's coming, nor have sorrow in our heart about a bad answer. Instead, there at the judgement we ourselves may boast of our deeds and of what our merits were.
I know that you were gloriously prospered in the worldly realm of this [?]
